articles.title: FX Daily: A dollar downturn lacks the rate ingredient
articles.author: Francesco Pesole, Frantisek Taborsky, Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
The post-midterm dollar correction requires a worsening of USD rate differentials to turn into a downturn. But as oil prices fall, other central banks are facing similar or even larger dovish repricing than the Fed. Data is key now, but indications are that they won’t turn USD-negative soon. Today, expect a hike in the UK and rate holds in Norway and Mexico
USD: Front-end rates should prevent a bigger decline
The Democratic sweep at the midterms delivered the negative dollar impact we had expected. But as we argued before the vote, we didn’t see a case for a bigger USD downturn. In our view, rates need to start moving against the dollar to justify a greater adjustment, unless idiosyncratic US asset underperformance fuels the move. But fears that a Democratic sweep would hit tech stocks didn’t materialise. Instead, a potential relief that the midterm risk event is out of the way, alongside plummeting oil prices, is fuelling an equity rally.
The key hurdle for a bigger USD downturn is that lower oil prices are not unequivocally USD-negative. Let’s look at yesterday’s moves in rates. As crude dropped 8%, two-year USD swap rates fell 5bp, broadly in line with CAD, AUD and SEK swaps. EUR, GBP and NZD 2yr swap rates, however, fell more, by around 8-10bp. To us, that is the most compelling argument against chasing the dollar much lower. Poorer US data and/or a more dovish Fed remain the necessary conditions for front-end USD rates to fall more than peers, and by extension for a broader USD downturn.
Instead, data has remained broadly supportive of Fed tightening expectations. Yesterday, the ISM services index was a tad softer than expected but remains well into expansionary territory. The employment subindex rose to 51.4, the highest since February. Paired with strong ADP payrolls at 86k, that’s likely to reinforce expectations for a robust payroll print tomorrow – consensus is 65k, but the whisper number has risen to 70k.
Today’s data highlights are the Challenger jobs cut figures for October and 3Q unit labour costs. We favour a stabilisation around 101.0-101.50 in DXY in the coming days, rather than another break lower.
Francesco Pesole
Elsewhere, Banxico announces its rate decision later today. The peso has been the worst-performing EM currency over the last two months after Banxico said it would not be following the Fed with a rate hike in September. In fact, some are looking for Banxico to heap more fuel on the peso’s fire with a rate cut today. Such a move could see USD/MXN push to 19. Either way, Banxico has slashed the peso’s rate protection to ultra-low levels, and the peso remains very vulnerable to global shocks.
Chris Turner
EUR: Knot pitches his hawkish agenda
Klaas Knot delivered a few remarks yesterday after the Netherlands officially backed his candidacy for the ECB presidency. He was firmly hawkish, claiming second-round inflation effects will probably pick up, and that the ECB will need to respond with higher rates to small shocks that will lift inflation. We’ll wait to hear from Pablo Hernández de Cos, who is the other frontrunner for the job, and a long-standing dove. An appointment of Knot would be a EUR-positive event given his hawkish views, in our view.
Meanwhile, eurozone inflation accelerated from 3.8% to 4.0% as expected in October. That brings the ECB closer to a December hike, as argued here by our macro team, even if core inflation remained anchored at 2.5%.
As mentioned in the USD section, the EUR:USD two-year swap rate gap widened against the euro yesterday as oil prices tumbled. A similar dynamic prevented EUR/USD from rallying in the summer when oil fell back to $70. Now, at least one more ECB hike – likely in December – looks like a done deal, providing a stronger floor for eurozone rate expectations. Still, this rate component, combined with lingering French risk, leaves us unexcited about a break higher in EUR/USD. We continue to see little upside potential beyond 1.130, our year-end target.
Francesco Pesole
GBP: BoE to resume tightening today
We expect the Bank of England to hike rates today by 25bp to 4.0% (full preview here ), in line with market expectations and consensus. A roughly 25% rise in household energy bills in January now looks increasingly likely, and we expect headline inflation to peak just above 4% early next year. That has often been indicated as the pain threshold for the BoE. Still, evidence of second-round inflationary effects remains limited.
We expect a 7-2 vote for a hike, and don’t see the BoE committing to further tightening at this stage. A follow-up move in February remains our base case, but policymakers should keep the emphasis firmly on incoming evidence of energy pass-through into wages and prices. An explicit signal that further hikes are likely would therefore constitute a hawkish surprise.
We think today’s hike can validate the pound’s recent gains, for now. However, a February hike is fully priced in, and the bar for a hawkish surprise lifting the pound seems fairly high. We don’t see immediate rebound potential for EUR/GBP, which is still dampened by the French effect, but GBP/USD is facing a less supportive short-term rate differential, as the GBP curve shows greater dovish flexibility when oil prices drop. We currently expect stabilisation around 0.840 in EUR/GBP, while Cable may see its upside capped at 1.350 in the near term.
Francesco Pesole
NOK: Norges Bank on hold today
Norges Bank should keep rates on hold today. Having been one of the quickest central banks to respond to fresh inflationary risks and given rates are already at an elevated 4.5%, the bar for further tightening remains fairly high. Incidentally, September CPI figures were a bit softer than expected, with underlying inflation staying at 3.0% and headline accelerating less than expected to 3.4%.
These are still elevated figures, so don’t expect Norges Bank to close the door to rate hikes yet. The threat of further action, if needed, will remain for some time, but we do not expect any further tightening in Norway, in line with Norges Bank’s September rate projections. Markets are pricing in just under 50% chances of another hike by March.
The krone is facing some headwinds due to the big drop in oil prices. However, it’s protected by much less hawkish pricing than other central banks, therefore facing less dovish pressure on energy price corrections. Yesterday, the NOK two-year swap rate dropped only 2bp. While this oil move can take EUR/NOK back to 10.50, a return to $80-85/bll may be needed for a return to the late September 10.90 levels. We see the pair ending the year in the 10.55-10.65 area.
In Sweden, following yesterday’s 25bp rate hike, inflation figures for October came in well below consensus. CPIF slowed more than expected to 1.1%, with the core measure excluding energy plummeting to 0.1% YoY from 0.5%. These were preliminary figures, and expectations are anyway of a pickup to above 2.0% in both CPIF and the ex-energy measure in 2027, in our view, justifying another hike in February. That likely explains the contained SEK reaction to the print. Still, these figures support our view of a consolidation around 11.00 in EUR/SEK as opposed to another big leg lower.
Francesco Pesole
CEE: Lower energy prices overshadow NBP and CNB meetings
In Poland, the NBP left interest rates unchanged at 3.75% yesterday, as expected, with the accompanying statement presenting a mixed picture. On one hand, the forecast included a significant upward revision to the inflation outlook; on the other, the statement noted lower core inflation in October and an anticipated economic slowdown in the third quarter of 2026. Notably, the NBP’s data cut-off point was likely two weeks ago. Consequently, the projections do not account for the downside surprise in October’s inflation figures, while they do reflect record-high energy prices, which, from today’s perspective, appear somewhat more favourable. Governor Adam Glapiński’s press conference today is expected to maintain a dovish tone, and we do not anticipate the NBP’s first rate hike until the first quarter of 2027.
In the Czech Republic, we expect the CNB to hike rates by 25bp to 4.00%, the second such increase since the onset of the US-Iran conflict. The CNB remains the most hawkish central bank in the CEE region, and its new forecast is expected to reinforce this stance. The updated projections will likely point to higher inflation, interest rates, and wages, alongside a hawkish external environment, while the GDP growth forecast will likely be revised downward. The CNB has scaled back its forward guidance. We do not expect firm commitments regarding future policy steps today, but rather an indication that the door remains open for further hikes if necessary. Given the rally in interest rates over the past few days, the threshold for a "hawkish" surprise is lower. The market is currently pricing in roughly 80bp of tightening, down from a peak of 125bp. That said, the CNB has generally delivered less hawkishness this year than the market anticipated, often resulting in a weaker currency and lower interest rates following its meetings.
The global narrative following the US midterms remains robust, and a sharp drop in oil prices could easily overshadow today’s meetings of the NBP and the CNB. This sense of relief is supporting CEE currencies and pushing rates lower. A dovish tone from the NBP should further fuel the decline in rates, while the zloty will likely retain room for recovery. The koruna is expected to underperform in this "risk-on" environment. We see less potential for gains here, given its lower beta and the fact that the CNB’s stance appears relatively neutral compared to current market pricing.
Frantisek Taborsky

articles.title: Czech National Bank review: The new neutral normal
articles.author: David Havrlant, Frantisek Taborsky
articles.fulltext:
The CNB increased the policy rate to 4%, in line with market expectations. However, the decision was very close, a 4-3 split. The new CNB forecast is revised toward a punchier inflation amid a softer economic expansion, implying a higher rates trajectory. We see 4% as the new normal, while further hikes will be restrained by dwindling economic activity
Punchier inflation amid mediocre economic performance
The CNB proceeded with a rate hike on Thursday, raising the base rate to 4%, which matches the expectations of market participants. The decision was taken in a split vote as four board members favoured a tighter monetary policy setup, while three policymakers opted for rate stability. The situation is perceived as inflationary, with persistently elevated core inflation, weaker exchange rate, and a still strong housing market, along with ample credit growth, seen as the main forces to keep in check through a tighter monetary policy stance. Robust wage growth and expansive fiscal policy are also assessed as risks to price stability. The decision and the mood of the press conference are in line with our expectations in both respects: i) one rate rise in November, and ii) concerns about economic performance putting a lid on further tightening.
CNB's real GDP path remains on the optimistic side
The new CNB staff projection points to slower economic expansion along with more elevated inflation, as we have foreseen. We must notice with some delight that the CNB inflation outlook is quite close to ING's view throughout the forecast horizon. Meanwhile, the CNB growth outlook remains a little optimistic compared with our view, especially for the coming year. As for short-term interest rate, the CNB forecast suggests a further increase up to 4.5% in the nearest future, followed by a gradual decline from 2Q27 to 3.5% at the end of 2028. We see such a trajectory rather as an alternative scenario, should inflation prove even stronger than in our forecast.
Forecast marriage in inflation
The interesting thing is that the governor described the monetary conditions as very tight at this point, and even beforehand. Well, should our hypothesis about the need for much higher equilibrium rates in the brave new world be right, then 4% seems to be a neutral stance that just prevents inflation from systematically hovering above the target. And with the CNB rate projection landing at 3.5% at the very end of the forecasting horizon, we believe that the staff is perhaps starting to drift in the same direction, at least implicitly.
That said, interest rates are an endogenous variable in the CNB workhorse model, so you can argue that this particular rate path enables the 2.5% economic expansion, with inflation receding towards the target. But hey, would you really be cutting rated so swiftly, while having inflation still running above your target and the economy growing around its potential? I have some doubts, but will stick to the old good maxim in dubio pro reo .
The bank board will likely smooth out the rates path
The infamous “all options are open” mantra was brought out of its shallow grave and into the daylight once again, but the dwindling real interest rate in the outlook does not suggest it stands on solid ground. Overall, we see 4% as the new neutral normal and believe that this will enable the CNB to ride out the wave of second-round effects, provided that our real GDP and inflation forecasts are right.
Our market view
The main takeaway from the CNB meeting is the 4–3 split within the board, following a long period of strong majorities. The market interprets this as a dovish signal, suggesting the CNB is unwilling to hike rates further unless the inflation situation deteriorates significantly. For the first time since the onset of the US-Iran conflict, the CNB’s forecast aligns closely with market pricing, with the PRIBOR rate peaking at around 4.55%. However, inflation is expected to worsen over the remainder of the year, approaching 3% and nearing 4% in the first quarter of 2027, bringing the new CNB outlook closer to our own forecast. We do not believe the current shift in energy prices justifies such a rally in CZK rates. The move appears excessive at this juncture. Consequently, we view two additional rate hikes as the minimum the market will tolerate, and, given today’s rebound, we anticipate a hawkish repricing.
EUR/CZK is facing renewed upward pressure. Indeed, if we take the shift in rate differentials at face value, the rates point toward 24.450. However, as previously noted, rates are likely to correct, as the current rate differential is too tight. Furthermore, the koruna benefits from strong seasonal support in November and December, which should help temper the current weakening pressure following the dovish CNB meeting. We therefore anticipate a new range of 24.350–24.400, little changed from our pre-meeting expectations.

Frantisek Taborsky

articles.title: Rates Spark: Bank of England likely to join the hiking club
articles.author: Benjamin Schroeder, Michiel Tukker
articles.fulltext:
A win for the Democrats helped Brent oil ease below $100, benefiting European government bonds. But we cannot ignore a 4% eurozone inflation reading, showing higher energy costs are already passing through the economy. The same story applies to the UK, where the Bank of England will likely hike rates. But with 24bp already priced in, this won't be a surprise
Euro rates like oil sliding below $100, but doesn't change 4% inflation reading
Market sentiment remains positive after Democrats won back both houses of Congress. The feed-through into European government bonds works via a noticeable easing in energy prices, with Brent sliding well below the US$100/bbl mark.
It eases the pressure on the ECB as markets see a greater chance that meaningful second-round effects can be avoided. Front-end inflation swaps have dropped noticeably over the past few sessions, and the money market curve now only expects a little more than 50bp of tightening by summer next year. There is still a contrast to printed inflation, where we saw headline inflation rise to 4% in October with yesterday’s release. We believe tensions will continue to be a source of volatility until time and data give markets more certainty about where we land.
Meanwhile in bond markets, 10y Bund yields slid below 3.3%. The 10y OAT/Bund spread has eased below 150bp, tightening more than 10bp on the day. We had pencilled in some spread tightening towards the end of the year mainly on the expectation that a 2027 budget showing some deficit consolidation will be passed, even if only by decree. But beyond that, the uncertainty ahead of the looming presidential election should leave spreads on wider levels still.
Higher energy prices force a hike from the Bank of England
With energy prices still elevated, we think inflation could reach 4% early next year, which means a hike by the Bank of England (BoE) is warranted. A hike today won’t come as a surprise, with 24bp already priced in, but we are less convinced about the need for more hikes thereafter. Markets take a more hawkish view and price in almost three more hikes after today.
We don’t expect a significant repricing of rates based on today’s meeting, as much will depend on inflation data. Markets have become less correlated with oil and we think each inflation release in the coming months will be anxiously watched for second-round effects. We think inflation dynamics should start improving by mid-2027, warranting the start of a big repricing lower for GBP rates .
Thursday’s events and market views
We start the day with French industrial production in September, for which consensus pencils in -0.3% YoY growth. Other interesting data includes eurozone PPIs for September, which is expected to increase by 10.6% YoY on the back of higher oil prices. From the US, we have challenger job cuts and weekly jobless numbers.
Spain will auction around €6.75bn across 5y, 10y and 14y SPGBs and a 7y SPGBei. France will auction €12bn across 10y, 12y, 17y and 31y OATs.

Authors
Benjamin Schroeder
Michiel Tukker

articles.title: A delayed landing for GBP rates
articles.author: Michiel Tukker
articles.fulltext:
GBP rates seem to have drifted too high versus Bank of England expectations, which we attribute to a significant risk premium stemming from prior trading trauma. We therefore see rates lower across the curve, but only once inflation risks settle and US rates ease lower. Meanwhile, structural supply factors will keep the sterling curve steeper
We expect domestic factors to pull rates lower in 2027, but global factors will continue to push gilt yields around. In our baseline forecast, we see the 10yr gilt yield easing lower as ugly inflation fears abate. The Bank of England could start considering rate cuts instead of more hikes. Looking back at the many global drivers pushing GBP rates around in 2026, we do think that the path lower will be volatile.
Easing UK inflation should bring rates lower, but global factors add volatility
The Bank of England’s policy rate is already much higher than those of its peers, which leads us to disagree with the significant amount of additional hiking priced in by markets. Forwards are now suggesting the Bank of England should hike at least 100bp, bringing the terminal rate to around 4.75%, above what markets are pricing for the Fed. The hawkish pricing already happened at the start of the surge in oil prices, but thus far, few rate hikes have materialised.
Markets keep overestimating the Bank of England’s appetite to hike
The excessively hawkish reaction feels like a trauma from being too dovish over the past few years. When we compare market pricing to actual policy changes, we see that expectations have been almost consistently wrong since 2023. Past inflation was, however, uglier than expected, easing more slowly than hoped. As a consequence, the Bank of England has only been able to cut policy rates very slowly since the easing cycle started in 2023.
Investors have been burnt many times on taking dovish GBP rate positions
Having been burnt many times over the past year, we think the front end of the GBP curve has built in a risk premium that stretches beyond macro fundamentals. We therefore see 2yr GBP rates easing lower into 1H27 as energy prices should start coming off their highs and inflation doesn’t surprise to the upside. But the bigger dovish turn will likely come in the second half as inflation numbers provide greater confidence about returning to the 2% target.
US rates add additional uncertainty to sterling rates
US dynamics cannot be ignored and should eventually also help sterling rates glide lower. The 10yr GBP swap rate can be modelled almost perfectly by Bank of England expectations and the US swap curve. These factors together explain some 98% of rate moves.
Two US ingredients are important: the level of the 10yr rate and the 2s10s slope of the curve. Our baseline forecast sees materially lower 10yr US rates, helping the 10yr gilt move lower in 2027.
Policy expectations and US rates account for 98% of 10Y GBP swap moves
But the US is facing inflation risks and a high deficit, adding uncertainty to the gilt outlook. If US inflation turns out to be more persistent than hoped, we could see the 10yr USD swap rate push toward 6%, spilling over to the sterling market. Similarly, concerns about global government debt and AI issuance can add to the upward pressure on global rates.
Changes in QT won’t stem the upward pressure on rates due to supply
While we think the UK is in a better position than most peers when it comes to "bad" government deficit and debt dynamics, supply pressures will continue to exert upward pressure on gilt yields. Thus far, the Bank of England has more actively reduced its balance sheet, adding to the supply for the private sector to absorb. Earlier this year we estimated that quantitative tightening (QT) added significant steepening pressure to sterling curves – more so than the Bank of England suggests.
The new approach to QT should ease the upward pressures on 30yr gilts, but the broader outlook remains the same. By keeping gilts on the balance sheet with maturities of 23 years or longer, markets no longer have to worry about absorbing that part of the curve. Having said that, the rise in 30yr yields is a global trend and not something on which the UK has a lot of influence.
Meanwhile, shorter maturities will still hit the market, albeit with a detour through the government Debt Management Office (DMO). The DMO could decide to shift gilt issuance to bills, but we doubt such a strategy will be pursued. Add a persistent budget deficit, and we should see supply pressures persist.
QT tweaks help 30yr gilts, but cannot revert a global trend of increased bond supply
The increased gilt supply is currently absorbed by relatively price-sensitive buyers. This increases upward yield pressure and can come with volatility. Banks are only absorbing part of the increase in supply, while insurance and pension funds are playing a smaller and smaller role, which is especially punitive for longer maturities. Foreign investors and other financials (i.e. asset managers, hedge funds) are picking up the slack. But these types of investors are more relative-value-focused and can be quick to sell if gilts start looking less attractive.
Gilts rely on price-sensitive buyers to pick up the increase in supply

articles.title: Euro rates have good reason to be nervous
articles.author: Michiel Tukker
articles.fulltext:
Easing inflation fears should bring euro rates down by mid-2027, but the path lower will be bumpy. We shift our attention from oil to inflation data and expect markets to react anxiously to upside surprises. Rising bond issuance outside the US government and AI could catch markets by surprise, but that is not our base case
Last year’s outlook was all about a stabilisation of euro rates, and boy, were we wrong. For 2027, we have no illusions of a calm ride. Our 2027 euro rates view combines substantial near-term upside risk with a more constructive year-end outlook.
Ugly second-round inflation fears could push the 10-year euro swap rate above 4%, while faster disinflation could take it towards 2%. Our baseline is that inflation pressures ease and the ECB terminal rate anchors near 2.5% by the end of 2027, although heavy global bond supply should keep long-dated rates relatively elevated.
Inflation is one of many uncertainties that can trigger different rate paths
For 2027, we shift our focus from oil to second-round inflation risks
Oil was the big story of 2026, but in 2027 we can no longer rely on the oil price to tell us where rates will go. Even if oil fell below $80/bbl, as assumed in our baseline, swap rates would not find much immediate relief. Instead, markets will watch each inflation reading anxiously for signs of second-round effects.
We take a relatively optimistic view in our baseline, but the upside risks to rates from inflation remain material. One bad reading could be enough to spook markets and risk a repeat of 2022-23, while it would take a series of benign inflation readings to convince markets of a more dovish tilt. We therefore see limited downside to rates in the first half of 2027. Only once there is sufficient evidence that second-round risks are limited do we turn more bullish on rates.
A tail risk for rates would be rising inflation combined with an inability of the ECB to stem the increase. Markets are pricing inflation in two years’ time (the 1Y1Y forward) at just 2.2%, suggesting strong confidence in the ECB’s ability to return inflation to target quickly. This is consistent with markets pricing in an aggressive further three ECB hikes. However, the effectiveness of monetary policy during supply shocks may be limited. Energy prices are still far from settled, and the global geopolitical landscape remains unstable.
Meanwhile, artificial intelligence investment is unlikely to respond to a few 25bp hikes when earnings growth is measured in double digits. A perceived weakening of monetary policy transmission, combined with upside inflation surprises, could push two-year euro swap rates another 100bp higher.
Markets remain very confident in the ECB’s ability to keep inflation close to target
A related risk would be a dovish shift in the ECB reaction function, effectively tolerating higher inflation to support the eurozone economy. The 5yr5yr inflation swaps suggest that markets price very little risk to the ECB’s commitment to the 2% target. At just 2.1%, the pricing is still well below the levels from before QE. France could, however, pose a challenge, as higher rates would trigger wider bond spreads, forcing the ECB to keep financial conditions supportive.
Quantitative tightening (QT) might be halted, and the ECB may simply have to accept higher inflation. Such a scenario does not appear to be priced by 5Y5Y inflation swaps. Brace for significantly steeper curves if this risk materialises.
An ECB forced to tolerate higher inflation looks like an unpriced risk
The US is crowding out the rest, pushing euro curves steeper
Longer-dated real rates are not anchored to central bank policy rates and are being pushed higher globally. The US is in the lead here, but the forces at work should be viewed in a global context. Quantitative tightening at all major banks continues to add bond supply that markets must absorb, pushing up longer-dated yields. Meanwhile, government debt is rising, adding to the issuance.
Global forces are pushing longer-dated rates higher, with no end in sight
We do not expect government bond supply trends to change overnight. We therefore think 10yr euro swap rates will remain relatively sticky at elevated levels, despite our baseline view of a move lower in 2yr rates. If the private sector also starts borrowing more, we may face even higher global rates. Corporates and households have been deleveraging since Covid, but the latest data may point to increased borrowing. This is not our baseline, as higher rates should weigh on investment appetite. The wildcard is artificial intelligence, which has driven investment in the US. Outside technology, however, the investment boom is not yet convincing.
US government debt is leading the credit cycle, but keep an eye on corporates
Fundamentals have not changed enough to warrant an entirely new normality
As economists, we want to see the economy return to a steady state, but such an equilibrium is now hard to pin down. We think markets in 2026 have gone too far in repricing the terminal ECB rate. An ECB rate settling above 3% is difficult to reconcile with the previous 1.75-2.25% range. Growth data have shown resilience, but the eurozone economy’s structural challenges remain. Although we still see significant near-term upside risks to rates, we expect rates to begin anchoring around an ECB terminal rate of about 2.5% by the end of 2027.
The sharp rise in the terminal ECB rate cannot be justified by macro changes
We do, however, think longer-dated rates are close to their historical fair value, limiting the downside potential for 10yr swap rates. Before the global financial crisis, 10yr rates were anchored around economists’ long-term nominal growth expectations. Fiscal austerity and quantitative easing pushed rates away from this equilibrium, but we are now close again to nominal growth expectations of 3.3%. Although artificial intelligence could boost productivity, in our baseline the increase is not material enough to produce a fundamentally different economic outlook.
The 10yr swap rate is close to fair value, limiting downside potential

articles.title: European bond spreads in a duel with the ‘Bad’
articles.author: Benjamin Schroeder
articles.fulltext:
Fiscal strains and election risks are putting eurozone bonds to the test. France is the key fault line, while Bunds’ safe-haven appeal masks mounting supply pressures. We see a turbulent first half of 2027, and any relief hinges on a credible path to French fiscal consolidation
European government bond markets – in a duel with the “Bad”
European government bond spreads have returned to the market’s focus. Importantly, spread moves are not purely idiosyncratic country stories. They also reflect broader risk sentiment, and higher interest rate volatility generally pushes spreads wider. At the onset of the Middle East turmoil, for instance, we saw sovereign spreads become more closely correlated with energy prices and expectations for European Central Bank rate hikes.
But high deficits – the “Bad”– and existing fiscal imbalances have made some countries more vulnerable than others, and these factors are increasingly shaping the dynamics of sovereign spreads. The “Bad” has re-entered the scene and is once again dominating the narrative in parts of the European government bond market.
While France is already being singled out as a risk factor with the potential to change the broader outlook for European sovereign debt, Europe’s busy election calendar suggests that idiosyncratic drivers could become more important overall. Spain goes to the polls later this month, and Italy will have to hold legislative elections before the end of next year. Finland will also hold parliamentary elections, while Germany faces elections in five federal states. And that is just to name the most prominent.
As markets navigate these political and fiscal risks, we expect spreads to remain at wider levels through much of the first half of the year.
Markets have reordered the EMU countries over the years, and have now singled out France
France – Facing the very “Bad”, the one that could change it all
Moody’s recently affirmed France’s last remaining double-A rating but maintained a negative outlook. The underlying assumption is that a 2027 budget containing at least some fiscal consolidation will eventually pass, even if this requires the use of a decree. That would represent a step in the right direction and could offer French government bond spreads some welcome relief going into the new year.
Beyond that, however, a “significant and sustained fiscal effort” will still be required. The outlook is clouded by the 2027 presidential election, with the two voting rounds on 18 April and 2 May. The far-right’s Marine Le Pen, the current leading contender, could subsequently call snap legislative elections in the summer in an attempt to break the parliamentary deadlock.
The benign scenario would be one in which Le Pen wins and follows through on her promises of fiscal consolidation. In that case, spreads could return towards levels seen before September, and France could conceivably trade tighter than Italy again. There is, however, still a long way to go before such an outcome can be taken for granted.
If Italy is the yardstick for a proper crisis, there is still room for escalation
The consolidation plans presented so far by Le Pen appear unrealistic, while the French public does not yet seem prepared to support the scale of adjustment that would ultimately be required. Against that backdrop, the market is likely to continue demanding a sizeable political risk premium. In the absence of positive catalysts, we see a 10-year OAT-Bund spread in the area of 150bp as a floor during the period of electoral uncertainty.
The tail risk is that public discontent instead translates into stronger support for the far left and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose proposals have included highly controversial ideas such as cancelling French debt held by the Bank of France. A greater probability being attached to such an outcome could push the 10-year OAT-Bund spread beyond 200bp.
More broadly, the absence of a credible multi-year consolidation plan, combined with the possibility of another hung parliament, would leave the door open to further sovereign rating downgrades, and not just from Moody’s. In an unscheduled update, Fitch only recently lowered the outlook of France’s A+ rating to negative. Under such circumstances, spreads could remain noticeably above 100bp even once the immediate electoral uncertainty has passed.
That said, we believe current spread levels already extend beyond what fundamentals alone would imply. The market is effectively pricing French debt as though it were already rated BBB. But prolonged and exceptionally high country-specific uncertainty, combined with elevated volatility in broader interest-rate markets, keeps valuations unattractive for many investors. One big risk is that structural foreign investors, which have historically been attracted by France's large, liquid bond market, start abandoning the credit. While data through August do not show any larger shifts, Japanese investors, for instance, have already shown themselves to be sensitive to French election risk in the past.
French has a large foreign investor base which has looked fickle around elections
The ECB can cap spreads, but does it want to?
In theory, the European Central Bank has both the instruments and the firepower to rein in sovereign spreads. But as long as the turmoil remains largely contained to France, we think the central bank will be inclined to let market mechanisms play out, thereby maintaining pressure on French politics to address the underlying fiscal issues. The ECB has historically been careful to avoid creating the impression of moral hazard.
If needed, the first and least targeted response would be to dial back hawkishness or even halt the tightening cycle. That might appear an easy way to calm markets. But as long as energy prices remain elevated and concerns about second-round inflation effects persist, there is a limit to how far the ECB would be willing to go solely in response to wider sovereign spreads.
A more targeted option would be to suspend quantitative tightening by resuming reinvestments. The ECB could even frame such a move as part of a broader adjustment of its balance-sheet policy, particularly as excess liquidity in the banking system approaches levels at which demand for central bank refinancing is expected to become more important. In theory, liquidity operations should take over at that stage. But as long as borrowing from the ECB continues to carry some stigma for banks, ending QT and resuming reinvestments could address two issues at once: easing pressure on sovereign bond markets while also slowing the decline in excess liquidity.
If turmoil were to spread further beyond France and threaten the transmission of monetary policy, the ECB could ultimately deploy its Transmission Protection Instrument. TPI comes with eligibility considerations, including compliance with the EU fiscal framework and debt sustainability, both of which would clearly matter in the case of France, although the ECB retains a degree of discretion in its assessment.
We think the bar for the ECB to actively intervene is high, however. By comparison, when the ECB intervened directly in Italian government bonds under the Securities Markets Programme in 2011, 10-year BTP-Bund spreads had moved beyond 500bp.
French bond spreads are already wider than fundamentals alone would imply
Germany hides in a temporary safe haven from the “Bad”
Germany sits at the opposite end of the spread spectrum from France. Bunds have reasserted their traditional role as a safe haven during the turmoil in French government bonds. During the geopolitical tensions at the start of the Iran conflict, evidence of such safe-haven demand had been fleeting. This time, the richness of Bunds looks more persistent because the turmoil goes to the heart of some of the monetary union’s longstanding vulnerabilities.
Yet the structural forces that had previously driven the cheapening of German government bonds have not disappeared.
Bond supply is likely to increase again as the government continues to roll out its investment and defence spending agenda. The German Finance Agency’s funding head has indicated that gross bond funding could exceed €400bn next year, around €50bn more than this year and making Germany the largest issuer of the union. Higher redemptions mean that the increase in net issuance is likely to be only around half as large. But the market must also absorb the German government bonds running off the ECB’s balance sheet. We estimate that this could add at least another €80bn to the amount the private sector needs to absorb over the coming year.
At the same time, political instability threatens the government’s reform agenda precisely when Germany needs to reset its economic model. An already fragile governing coalition will face five state elections, four of them concentrated in April and May and the other in September.
Once the immediate flight-to-quality premium fades, we expect 10-year Bunds to cheapen back to at least 20bp over OIS, from around 13bp currently. Domestic fiscal and political factors could push the spread wider still by the end of the year.
10y Bund safe haven dynamics outweigh structural issues for now
2027, likely a showdown in two parts
The first half of next year will still be dominated by eurozone political risk. France’s 2027 budget might offer temporary but welcome relief at the start of the year, when an important funding window traditionally opens for many issuers beyond the government bond market.
The second half of the year may offer relief from the turmoil, largely contingent on the outcome of the French elections and whether a new president can offer a credible path towards fiscal consolidation. But at that point, Germany, as a core issuer, becomes exposed again to its domestic structural cheapening factors.

articles.title: Bank of England set for first rate hike as energy shock worsens
articles.author: James Smith, Michiel Tukker, Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
We expect a 7-2 vote to hike rates this week and, barring a collapse in energy prices, we think a follow-up move in February is likely too. However, market pricing for the Bank of England still looks extreme
Higher energy prices set to push inflation above 4%
The Bank of England has so far managed to avoid a rate hike since the start of the Iran war, but that’s about to change. We, like most, expect a hike at its 5 November meeting, and think a follow-up move in February is more likely than not.
Why now? Until now, the Bank would argue it’s been on “active hold”. It was set to cut rates by upwards of 50 basis points this year, so simply not doing that amounted to de facto tightening. By that logic, the Bank has added a similar amount of policy restriction as the European Central Bank, which has lifted its deposit rate twice.
But the worsening energy crisis has made it much harder for the Bank not to act. The spike in natural gas prices means inflation is set to take another leg higher into winter. A circa 25% rise in the regulated cap on household energy bills in January is all but baked in.
We expect headline CPI to peak a touch above 4% early next year, and we think the BoE's new forecasts will show this too. The Bank’s July projections had inflation reaching 3.2% in late 2026, based on oil below US$80/bbl and natural gas at around half its current level.
Energy prices have risen significantly since the Bank's July forecasts
The Bank is set to hike rates for insurance purposes
4% is an important line in the sand for the BoE. Last summer, the Bank set out research suggesting that second-round effects become more likely once inflation surpasses this level. We suspect this is still front of mind for many officials.
Then again, there is essentially no sign of these much-feared second-round effects so far. Away from motor fuel, inflation has been in line with the Bank’s July forecasts. Our measure of 'energy-intensive' inflation has actually fallen this year, even after accounting for one-off changes in water bills and car tax.
One of the Bank’s favoured measures of ‘core services’ inflation, which strips out volatile and indexed categories, is well-behaved too. And though it has likely bottomed out, private-sector wage growth at 3.4% year-on-year is hardly problematic . Despite signs of stabilisation in the jobs market, there’s little evidence wage pressures are set to build.
True, growth has been much better than feared. But then the Bank has often taken a more sceptical view of the GDP numbers, preferring to look at more benign survey-based measures of activity.
This all leaves the Bank in a strange situation: hiking not because the economic data is telling it to, but because of the risks presented by sharply higher energy prices. The energy crisis has reached sufficient depth and longevity that officials likely feel they, reluctantly, have to act.
'Energy-intensive' inflation hasn't picked up
The key things to watch
So what should we watch at the November meeting?
First, the vote split. We know there are two doves, Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor, who are deeply sceptical of the need for higher rates. But we suspect the other seven committee members will back a hike. Could there be more dissenters? Governor Andrew Bailey hasn’t sounded hugely enthusiastic about hiking, though a governor has only dissented twice since 1997 and both times in the financial crisis.
So if there is extra dissent, Sarah Breeden looks the most likely candidate, having stressed that most businesses are absorbing the energy shock rather than raising prices. Dave Ramsden is another, less likely, candidate.
Second, there’s the forward guidance. We think the Bank will be as non-committal as possible. Something like: “The Committee will carefully assess the extent to which higher energy prices are propagating into wage and price-setting. The timing and pace of any further increases will depend on the evolution of the inflation outlook. Monetary policy is not on a pre-set path.”
That’s a clever way of saying: we could hike again, but it’s not inevitable.
If there’s going to be a hawkish surprise, it would be if the Bank says something like “some further tightening in monetary policy is likely to be appropriate over the coming months”.
Another rate hike in February seems to be the growing consensus – and our own view too. There’s little precedent for ‘one-and-done’ rate rises. But it’s one thing thinking that, another saying it out loud. There’s a lot that can happen between now and February. And having made a hawkish misstep all the way back in March, when the Bank sounded open-minded about tighter policy, opening the floodgates for markets to price in rate hikes, it’ll want to tread carefully here.
A more dovish formulation would be if the Bank makes further hikes explicitly contingent on second-round effects: one hike as an insurance move, but anything more requiring solid data. For example, “If there were evidence of more persistent second-round effects in wage and price-setting, further tightening in monetary policy would be required”.
Finally, watch the individual member paragraphs tucked away in the minutes. Does anyone formally push back against market pricing, which has more than four hikes priced by this time next year? Even Chief Economist Huw Pill, one of the hawks, has recently indicated that such pricing looks unlikely.
The impact on rates markets
Even if the Bank does choose to push back, will markets listen?
A simple model of two-year swap rates against oil, natural gas, equity markets and the equivalent USD and EUR rates shows that these global factors are explaining less of the daily movement in sterling rates than they were over the summer.
Global factors are explaining less of GBP rates moves
Indeed, the dovish repricing that we’ve seen for the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank has not been mirrored in the UK. Perhaps it’s because Britain lacks a story like France has or, in America’s case, AI fears. But robust UK growth data may also be playing a role. Economic surprise indices have been touching multi-year highs.
Still, UK swap rates remain deeply correlated with oil prices. And barring a big surprise, and with more than 100bp of hikes already priced, it’s hard to see the Bank triggering a substantial repricing of rate expectations at this meeting.
GBP rates remain positively correlated with oil - unlike EUR rates
The impact on the pound
Sterling is trading reasonably well, helped by the view that high energy prices leave the Bank of England no alternative but to hike rates on Thursday.
Upside economic surprises, UK fiscal policy seemingly heading in the right direction and warmer ties with the EU all seem to be helping sterling too. Notably, speculators are still running reasonably large short positions in sterling, which suggests this period of sterling outperformance can continue.
EUR/GBP has come a long way very quickly – a near 4% drop in a little over a month. Some consolidation is probably due. But with high energy prices likely to keep expectations of higher UK policy rates in place until early next year and French budgetary problems unresolved, it is too early to expect a significant low in EUR/GBP.

articles.title: Bank of Japan hits 2% price target
articles.author: Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
In a big day for monetary policy in Japan, the Bank of Japan finally announced it had hit its 2% price target – a target set in 2013. The question now for markets is how quickly the BoJ takes the policy rate to neutral. We now think it will hike in December and March. A hawkish BoJ can help keep a lid on USD/JPY at 160
CPI is consistent with price stability target
In its October outlook report released today, the Bank of Japan finally got to say that "underlying CPI inflation is at a level that is generally consistent with the price stability target of 2%, and is expected to remain at around that level." That was a target set in 2013 and one the BoJ has battled to hit after decades of deflation.
In terms of what that means for monetary policy from here, the clear message is to expect further tightening. The debate now shifts to how quickly the BoJ takes rates to neutral, seen in the 1.75-2.00% area.
For today, the policy rate was left at 1.25%, as back-to-back hikes could have upset markets. But running through the new Outlook Report were three themes that the BoJ felt could all contribute to upside price risks: energy prices, AI demand and the weak yen. In that report, growth forecasts were left around 0.7-0.8% (near or above potential), while CPI forecasts were revised slightly higher.
There remained several references to labour shortages and a confidence that strong corporate profits would be feeding into wages and higher inflation. There was also an acknowledgement that interest rates were rising overseas and presumably a fear that a failure to track Federal Reserve and European Central Bank rate hikes in December could leave the yen vulnerable again.
We now think the BoJ will hike rates by 25bp in both December and March and will probably be comfortable with a policy rate around 1.75% ahead of further government measures to support consumption next April.
What was slightly surprising was the BoJ announcing an acceleration in its ETF sales as it tries to unwind its balance sheet and improve market functioning. After running at JPY330bn per year since 2025, ETF sales will be accelerated to JPY860bn per year starting in 2027. This looks to be a sign of confidence in the Japanese economy from the BoJ.
BoJ's latest growth and inflation forecasts
Market reaction
USD/JPY was slightly softer amid a broadly weaker dollar today. The market already prices the BoJ policy rate being taken to 2.00% next summer, meaning that today’s hawkish BoJ communication was no surprise. 10-year Japanese government bond yields have matched the drop in US Treasury yields this month, and their outperformance of Treasuries since July must be welcome news to policymakers in Tokyo.
Barring the US midterms or a sizeable AI correction taking a big chunk out of the dollar, we expect USD/JPY to stay bid towards the upper end of a 155-160 range over the coming months. We do not see USD/JPY turning decisively lower until the second quarter next year, when we look for the dollar to turn.
The surprise package here could be that USD/JPY does a USD/KRW – where AI demand fires up broader domestic demand growth in Japan, confidence grows in the domestic economy, and more portfolio and trade flows are brought home. One to watch in 2027.

articles.title: Bank of Canada likely to hike again after today’s move
articles.author: James Knightley, Francesco Pesole
articles.fulltext:
The BoC raised the policy rate by 25bp to 2.5% today, matching market expectations. Policymakers acknowledge rising inflationary risks, and while not recommitting to a rate path, the indications are that this won’t be a one-and-done hike. We expect the next move in 1Q27, with risks of an earlier one in December. We remain cautious on CAD's upside risks
BoC to proceed carefully after hike
The Bank of Canada has raised its target for the overnight rate by 25bp to 2.5%. Ahead of the meeting, it was about 80% priced by markets, with economists split down the middle on whether we would get a hike or not – the Canadian outlook is improving, but inflation is in line with target and the recent jobs numbers have been disappointing with the unemployment rate rising to 6.5%.
The statement justifies the action on the basis that the recent growth figures have been stronger than anticipated thanks in part to "solid" consumer spending, while business capex in the oil and gas industry has rebounded on higher energy prices. They also note that sectors that had been heavily impacted by US tariffs have strengthened.
In an environment of rising cost pressures, which so far have been largely absorbed by businesses, there is a sense that cost pass-through could be more of a theme for 2027. As such, inflation could be more persistent than previously thought likely. Given this situation, the BoC concluded that "there could be the need to increase the policy rate further..." but they will "proceed carefully".
Market expectations still too hawkish
Markets are currently seeing the next meeting in December as a 50:50 call on whether we get another hike. Right now our forecast is for the BoC to hike rates to 2.75% in the first quarter of 2027 (our preference is January over March) and hold them steady, but the risk is that they go a little more aggressively, and we see a December hike followed by a 1Q27 move.
Anyway, we still judge market expectations for 90bp of tightening over the next 12 months as overly hawkish. The BoC has a central estimate for the neutral rate around 2.75%, and we agree with their estimate that second-round effects will be present but overall contained, especially in terms of wage growth spillover.
CAD outlook is very oil-dependent
In the near term, elevated oil prices risk prompting an upward surprise in inflation and leading markets to price in a December hike. The BoC can accommodate this. This adds to the weight that oil prices have on CAD’s near-term outlook. We remain on the more bearish side of the oil story, and think a decline in energy prices could lead to broad dovish repricing and release pressure on the BoC to hike in December.
We remain unconvinced that CAD can draw much more benefit from the domestic story, and only see USD/CAD trading steadily below 1.40 should USD-related risks build up. Our target for year-end for the pair remains unchanged, with some upside risks to 1.420.

articles.title: Fed holds rates steady despite inflation being too high
articles.author: James Knightley, Padhraic Garvey, CFA, Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged that progress is being made, but inflation remains too high and a December FOMC rate hike remains our call
10-2 vote to keep policy unchanged
The Federal Reserve voted 10-2 in favour of leaving the Fed funds target rate range at 3.75%-4%. Only 2bp of a potential 25bp hike was priced ahead of the decision and only 6 of 97 organisations polled by Bloomberg predicted a hike, so this was no surprise and market reaction has been limited.
Senior Fed officials, including Vice Chairs Philip Jefferson and Michelle Bowman and Governor Chris Waller, suggested ahead of the decision that they were prepared to move cautiously, seeing little need for back-to-back rate hikes after September's policy change. Nonetheless, Beth Hammack and Lisa Cook both felt that the current situation warranted additional action. Cook’s vote for a hike was a surprise given the general sense that she was a centrist, and it will do nothing to improve her fraught relationship with President Trump. Instead, we had suspected it would be one or both of Neel Kashkari and Lorrie Logan (who both also dissented in July) that would join Hammack in voting in favour of a further rate hike.
There aren’t many changes in the accompanying press release, with the economy described as “expanding at a strong pace” and “inflation remains elevated”. There was no pre-commitment to further action, with it being the data that “will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
At the press conference, Kevin Warsh offered no real guidance other than to say that inflation remains too high, but the overwhelming consensus in the FOMC is that the “medicine” is starting to work. Moreover, the Fed will deliver price stability, “no ifs, ands or buts." He did state that from next September one FOMC meeting won’t have a rate vote, leaving it to focus exclusively on monetary policy strategy. From 2028, this will become two meetings, leaving only six meetings at which interest rate decisions will be made.
US inflation and unemployment
December rate hike remains the most likely path
There is the valid question that, given a majority of FOMC members project a rate hike before the end of the year, why didn’t they take that decision today? Kevin Warsh’s response was that he himself didn’t make a prediction and, in any case, they removed some policy accommodation in September. Inflation is “going the right way” and he is encouraged by the progress made.
We will have two jobs reports and one inflation print ahead of the December decision. The November CPI will be released the day after the Fed meeting, and officials will almost certainly get to see it. As such, they will have more information than the market does, meaning a surprise can’t be completely ruled out. For now, a December hike looks a solid bet, which would leave the Fed funds target rate range at 4.00%-4.25%.
The sharp move higher in Treasury yields and the firmer dollar are tightening financial conditions to a degree, but our forecast path for the Fed assumes that in the couple of months following the midterm elections we see an agreement that improves the flow of energy from the Persian Gulf, but significantly, allows for a sharp reduction in shipping and insurance costs. It's the latter point that is crucial to delivering lower pump prices at a time when refineries are working at capacity.
If correct, this should meaningfully ease inflation pressures, and with US wage growth (the biggest cost input for corporate America) looking very benign at just 3% and the largest component of the inflation basket – housing at 35% by weight – set to experience more disinflation, we believe overall US inflation can fall back to 2% in the second half of 2027.
Hence, we subsequently anticipate a prolonged pause through to December 2027, when we have that December 2026 hike being reversed. This is in line with the current consensus forecast, while the Fed’s own projections (its central forecast) see one hike this year with rates left unchanged throughout 2027.
The lean hawkish is enough to validate the break back above 5% for the 10yr
Hardly a word in the short statement that is not leaning hawkish. But no hike. Prior to the FOMC meeting, it was remarkable how the 10yr yield had been clinging to the 4.99% level. It was like a comfort level; technically below 5%, but not too far below in case it needs to turn tail and shoot back up again. It seemed that the US 10yr was waiting to tick off this outcome before deviating too much from 5%. Well, it’s now had the outcome. The initial reaction was up. But the reaction to Chair Warsh’s words at the press conference was to revert down to 5%, and briefly below. This can be rationalised by Warsh’s comforting words on inflation expectations, which he deemed to have been tamed somewhat.
That all being said, our interpretation is that this Fed still has a job to do if the type of price stability that Chair Warsh has described is to be achieved. He has described price stability as strictly 2%, and he seems to be serious about hitting that. This is good from a protective sense for the back end. At the same time, it’s tough to view the current set-up of still elevated printed inflation and a Fed on hold as all that protective. Also, inflation expectations in fact rose post the Fed decision and subsequent Warsh commentary. We glean from this enough to validate the move back above 5% on the 10yr. We maintain our view that we’re on a journey back up in the direction of 5.25%.
The implementation note was broadly unchanged in terms of action. The various implementation rates are unchanged, as are the implementation mechanisms. And the Fed will continue to reinvest principal payments from its MBS securities into Treasury bills. We’re likely still some way from the Fed spelling out a plan to shrink its balance sheet, which we know remains a policy objective for Chair Warsh. We expect recommendations from the various committees to surface closer to the turn of the year. Meanwhile, liquidity conditions are stable, with repo behaving far better than it did a year ago.
Dollar softens a touch
Perhaps it was a belated acknowledgement that there would not be forward guidance on a December rate hike, but the lack of clarity there seemed to weigh on short-dated rates and the dollar. Chair Warsh actually sounded a little uncomfortable when a reporter asked whether the current policy setting was sufficient for the Fed to hit its goals.
The dollar reaction – a slight softening – probably owed to positioning. Here the consistent run higher in energy prices over recent months, solid US activity and French budget woes have largely seen one-way traffic in the dollar since early September.
However, the overall tone of the press conference, strong and broadening US growth and above-target inflation, suggests the dollar does not need to correct much at all at this stage.
Up next will be the ECB meeting on Thursday and the Bank of Japan meeting on Friday. Barring major hawkish surprises at either of those meetings, we would expect the dollar to continue to consolidate towards the top of recent ranges.

articles.title: EMEA FX Talking: External headwinds up against local stories
articles.author: Rafal Benecki, Peter Virovacz, David Havrlant, Mateusz Sutowicz, Dmitry Dolgin, Muhammet Mercan, Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
Like many emerging market currencies, those in the EMEA region have been hit by higher US Treasury yields and the stronger dollar. Yet the domestic stories look constructive for many, and a combination of some local rate hikes as well as light foreign positioning (ex Hungary) can insulate these currencies from the global bond market sell-off
Main ING EMEA FX Forecasts
EUR/PLN: Zloty swings with market sentiment
EUR/PLN has moved towards 4.40 after trading around the 4.30 level during summer. With market sentiment deteriorating amid geopolitical tensions in Iran, France and Russia, the coming weeks could challenge the zloty.
PLN has recently strengthened its correlation with EUR/USD, so the dollar’s future moves will be the key driver in the currency’s performance, while domestic factors are likely to take a back seat.
We retain a broadly positive stance on the zloty in the medium term due to solid GDP momentum and persistent outperformance. However, the balance of risks has become less favourable; the National Bank of Poland may deliver fewer hikes than priced, and a hot budget debate could reveal vulnerabilities.
EUR/HUF: A credibility boost is in the making for the forint
While EUR/HUF has shown some volatility recently, the swings have been far more moderate than we used to see. This reflects general positioning and the euro adoption story.
We think an idiosyncratic shock is coming with the 2027 budget and the mid-term fiscal consolidation plan. If the government delivers a credible plan, as we expect, and announces official talks on joining ERM II, this could provide a credibility boost to the forint.
A significant drop in the risk premium and some insulation from geopolitical market turbulence could take EUR/HUF down to the 350-355 area over the next month. This would, however, reopen the door to a National Bank of Hungary easing cycle starting in December, putting the HUF on a mild depreciation path over the following 12 months.
EUR/CZK: Braving the turbulence
The Czech Republic has also been affected by the global bond yield rally, with the turmoil applying depreciation pressure on the koruna. Inflation is set to increase on the back of rallying import prices and second-round effects of the oil price shock starting to bite.
We believe that equilibrium interest rates are higher than generally assumed, since the cost of capital must adjust to a world of protracted conflict and increased resource scarcity. A higher base rate is warranted to prevent the koruna from weakening further, which would exacerbate domestic price pressures.
That said, the ECB may turn more hesitant despite elevated inflation, as concerns over French fiscal issues rekindle fears of another euro crisis. In turn, the real interest rate differential should help the koruna withstand the turmoil and gradually appreciate once things have calmed down.
EUR/RON: Rating downgrade avoided, RON still vulnerable
EUR/RON had its second major move of the year, climbing from 5.28 to 5.35, which looks to be the near-term level. Official interventions have likely moderated the impact of significant outflow pressures through both September and so far in October – with the fear of rating downgrades and the protracted political instability as key drivers.
While the rating remained in place, the political arena is yet to find its consensus. The key positive element supporting the credit story remains the budget deficit, which stood at 2.89% of GDP as of August 2026 (vs 4.50% in August last year).
A tighter liquidity management has recently led FX implied yields to the highest levels since May 2025, although funding pressures have diminished from their early October peak. We expect the pair to remain around its current levels by year-end and close next year near 5.45.
EUR/RSD: RSD stable ahead of parliamentary elections
EUR/RSD has remained relatively flat in the range of 117.3–117.5. Yet again, the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has extended the operating waiver for Serbia's NIS refinery until 30 October. The NIS ownership issue is yet to be resolved.
Snap parliamentary elections have been called for 25 October, with President Aleksandar Vucic resigning in order to pursue premiership. The fiscal deficit has recently been revised higher, from 3.0% to 3.5% of GDP in 2026, mainly reflecting higher social expenditure.
At its October meeting, the National Bank of Serbia kept the key rate in place at 5.75%, continuing to highlight inflation uncertainty. Between January and August, the Bank sold €407m to keep the pair stable. We expect the pair to remain around the current levels ahead.
USD/UAH: NBU efforts to protect the UAH
The hryvnia remained under pressure as the dollar strengthened, partly due to renewed Middle East tensions. Consequently, USD/UAH temporarily broke above 45.0, reaching its highest level on record.
Hryvnia depreciation could have been sharper, but National Bank of Ukraine action provided support. In September, the central bank raised rates by 50bp to 16.0% and maintained sizeable FX interventions, with the four-week average near record highs.
The outlook for the hryvnia appears cloudy as the macroeconomic environment remains challenging – particularly as the ongoing war with Russia poses an increasing threat to the Ukrainian economy.
USD/KZT: Growing state FX sales backlog to boost KZT resilience
The tenge gained 5% against the US dollar in September, driven mainly by private capital inflows, particularly continued non-resident demand for KZT government bonds.
Combined net FX sales by the state oil fund (NFRK) and National Bank of Kazakhstan fell to zero in September, compared with $1.0–1.3bn per month in 1H26. As NFRK sales have remained below fiscal financing needs since mid-2026, an estimated $1.0–1.5bn backlog of FX sales has accumulated.
After gaining 25% YoY against USD, the tenge has limited upside, particularly amid global risk aversion and regional geopolitical uncertainty. At the same time, Kazakhstan’s high real rates should continue to attract carry-trade inflows, while the eventual release of the state FX sales backlog could ensure KZT resilience if market sentiment deteriorates.
USD/UZS: Still waiting for gold exports to catch up
After appreciating 1% against the US dollar in August, the soum was broadly flat in September and early October. This was slightly weaker than we expected, but still resilient given the global dollar rally and lower gold prices.
Gold exports remain a key variable for Uzbekistan’s FX market. There were no exports in August, and gold was exported only in April and July this year. Year-to-date volumes stand at just 18 mt, implying a substantial backlog compared with 85 mt in FY25 and the historical annual range of 80–120 mt.
Like Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan offers high real rates and is likely to continue doing so despite a potential monetary policy easing. As inflation has stabilised at 6.2–6.4% YoY, we see some room for a cautious cut from the current 14.00% policy rate before the end of the year.
USD/TRY: Rate cut expectations build as inflation eases
Fund volatility has not affected the dollarisation ratio. Net outflows in lira-denominated funds turned TRY625bn between the end of August and 6 October, excluding suspended funds. Meanwhile, outflows from FX-linked fund assets totalled $2.2bn, while higher TRY deposits and repo balances suggest dollarisation remains contained.
September’s CPI came in below consensus, supported by favourable food and transport. Annual CPI fell to 29.7% from 31.5% in August. Seasonally adjusted CPI, a key indicator closely monitored by the Central Bank of Turkey, slowed to 1.6% month-on-month from 2.2% in August, marking one of the lowest readings seen in recent years.
This backdrop increases the likelihood of a shift toward policy rate cuts. The recent investment fund disruption is likely to raise downside risks to activity. Given September’s CPI and weak domestic demand, we expect two 100bp cuts in October and December.
USD/ZAR: A resilient performance from the rand
The high-yield rand has been one of the better EM performers during the sell-off over the last month. Its fiscal metrics are not particularly great, (5% budget deficit, 80% debt to GDP), but the coalition government looks to be taking things in the right direction; a primary budget surplus is helpful here.
The South African Reserve Bank is helping out too, having hiked 25bp in September to 7.25%. It is threatening to hike rates again on a baseline view that core central banks hike another 50bp.
A difficult external environment suggests USD/ZAR may need to trade in a 16.00-16.60 range for the next three to six months. As 2027 progresses, however, the case for sub-16.00 levels builds.
USD/ILS: Israel’s higher credit rating provides a buffer
Israel’s high-quality credit rating (A-) has provided a buffer to the shekel during this debt crisis. That largely stems from Israel’s strong external investment position and relatively large domestic capital market. Additionally, the debt sell-off has yet to unhinge the US tech story – of which the shekel is a beneficiary.
In September, the Bank of Israel cut rates to 3.25%, citing low inflation. Markets currently price further aggressive cuts to the 2.00% area, which seems excessive. The BoI might prefer to save those rate cuts for when the dollar is broadly softer – maybe in 2Q27 – and when USD/ILS is threatening to run away sub-3.00.
Longer term, the trade-weighted ILS is very firm, and we suspect Israeli authorities will struggle to tolerate much further strength.
